literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's literary offerings are full of voices, from butlers and albino boys to a mother in working-class Scotland, with a little poetry and some very old verse to finish.

Let me begin with character and narrators, which I know is your territory. The Paris Review has a piece called "Kazuo Ishiguro, Unlocked: The Butler as Metaphor", about how Ishiguro goes about inhabiting his characters. Only a short excerpt was available, but the idea of the butler as a way into a whole method of writing feels like something you could take straight into a première classroom. On a more playful note, BBC Radio 4's Bookclub has Matt Haig talking to readers about The Midnight Library. You will know the premise: Nora Seed moves through a library of alternative lives. It is very much a novel carried by its narrator, and hearing readers question the author about her is a pleasure in itself.

Literary Hub has two pieces on Agnes Owens and her novel A Working Mother. Megan Nolan writes an appreciation that she frames as an ode to working-class Scotland, and Lit Hub's daily digest points to a critical essay that finds "the surrealness of everyday life" in its pages. That phrase alone made me want to pick the book up. It is a lovely example of a writer from outside the usual literary milieu, and of a voice you could step into without needing to know the culture beforehand. Literary Hub also offers the opening of a short story called "Hyena Boys", which follows Bonaventure, an albino boy who is mocked and has long kept away from the world. It is only an excerpt, but the character is vivid and the prose promises a story you could enter at once.

And from the Southeast Review comes an assessment of Arundhati Roy's Mother Mary Comes to Me, her memoir of her mother. The text I saw was slight, but the title, "This is Arundhati, My Dear", suggests a personal and lyrical book about a formidable woman.

Now to prose style. The New York Times reviews Annie Proulx Stories, a career-spanning collection of her short fiction. The reviewer notes her dense, thorny prose, and that is exactly the appeal: sentences you have to slow down for, and sharp characters who come out of them. Bookmunch, meanwhile, reviews Hermione Lee's biography Anita Brookner: Art and Life, which looks at the novelist's life alongside her art and at attempts to restore her reputation. Anything by Hermione Lee is worth attention, and the question of how a writer's reputation is rebuilt is interesting in its own right.

Then there is something more divisive. The Guardian reviews Tom McCarthy's new experimental novel, The Rhyl Poster. It follows a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency through a hallucinatory crisis, in what the paper calls an avant-garde spy drama. The reviewer is frustrated by the riddles and asks whether they are worth it. I would read it less as a verdict than as an invitation to the argument over whether McCarthy's method pays off. It could make a good talking point for older pupils thinking about difficulty in fiction.

On to history and the ways stories carry it. Mary Beth Keane talks to Literary Hub about Whale Harbor, her fifth novel, which follows the Irish diaspora from County Cork to Galveston in the nineteenth century. She also draws on her own family lineage, which gives the migration story a personal weight. It sounds like the kind of novel that teaches history better than a textbook chapter. Also on Literary Hub, there is an essay on how African literature treats the boundary between the living and the dead. Ancestors and spirits are presented not as fantasy but as part of lived reality, which offers a way into a culture from within, through story.

Another essay there, by a novelist, describes how Derek Walcott's postcolonial epic helped her write her own book. It places Walcott within the classical tradition, and it notes how Luis Rafael Sánchez recast Sophocles' Antigone in a fictional Caribbean republic. If you enjoy seeing how old stories get reborn in new places, this one is for you.

Staying with the very old, Backlisted has rerun its Hallowe'en episode on Beowulf, first broadcast in twenty twenty. It is a long, lively conversation comparing the translations by Seamus Heaney, Tolkien, Michael Morpurgo and Maria Dahvana Headley, and how the poem's language has been rendered over the centuries. With a dark evening and a cup of tea, it sounds ideal listening, and a fine way to hear how much a translator's choices shape the music of a line.

Finally, some poetry and atmosphere. Literary Hub's roundup of new poetry for November is led by Malgorzata Lebda's collection Mer de Glace, translated by Mira Rosenthal. The opening lines quoted are lyrical, and the translator's notes are mentioned as part of the appeal. A title like that will make you think of mountains and ice, which may feel close to home in Belledonne. The same site also has a short, atmospheric passage set on a bay at sunset, around Shep's Island, which seems to open a longer piece called "The Shared Life of Egan and Lucian". The text was thin, but the prose is lovely and may reward a few quiet minutes.

That is the shelf for today, Yamuna, and I hope something on it keeps you company over your next coffee.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a rich couple of days in the literary pages, with plenty of strong voices, some lovely language, and a few pieces that connect novels to history and to older stories.

Let me begin with characters and voices from outside the usual literary circles, since several pieces today turn on exactly that. Literary Hub has an appreciation by Megan Nolan of Agnes Owens's novel A Working Mother, which she presents as an ode to working-class Scotland. The same publication's daily digest from the second of November carries a critical essay on the book too, and that one says it finds "the surrealness of everyday life" in its pages. That phrase is worth holding on to. It suggests a novel where ordinary routines, in the right hands, turn strange and slightly dreamlike. Two writers turning to the same book in the same week is a good sign, and if you've never come across Owens, this might be the moment. The digest also includes children's book recommendations for November, which may be useful if you ever want something for younger readers at the lycée or at home.

Staying with vivid characters, Literary Hub has published the opening of a short story called "Hyena Boys". It follows Bonaventure, an albino boy who is mocked and has long avoided the world. It's only an opening excerpt, but the character comes through straight away, and it looks like the kind of story you can step into without needing any background. A boy who has kept the world at arm's length is a promising place to start.

And in the New York Times, there's a review of a career-spanning collection, Annie Proulx Stories. The reviewer notes her dense, thorny prose, and I think that's a fair description of her appeal. Her sentences are packed and a little prickly, and they reward being read slowly, almost like a piece of music with some awkward, wonderful intervals. A career-spanning volume lets you hear how that style develops over time, and it brings together all those sharply drawn characters in one place.

Now to narrators and the craft of inhabiting a character. The Paris Review has an essay called "Kazuo Ishiguro, Unlocked: The Butler as Metaphor". The excerpt I have is brief, but the piece is about Ishiguro's method and how he gets inside his characters, with the butler serving as a kind of metaphor. If you teach The Remains of the Day or anything like it, the idea of the narrator as someone defined by service, restraint and what goes unsaid is rich ground for a class on unreliable or self-deceiving voices. I can't tell you more than that about the essay's argument, but the framing alone is promising.

On a very different note, BBC Radio 4's Bookclub has Matt Haig talking about The Midnight Library. The novel follows Nora Seed through a library of alternative lives, so each book on the shelf is a different version of her existence. It's a strongly narrator-led story, and the Bookclub format, where the author talks with readers, tends to bring out how a writer thinks about character and structure. It could make a nice companion if you want something to listen to on the way down the valley.

There's also a review in the Guardian of Tom McCarthy's new experimental novel, The Rhyl Poster. It follows a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency through a hallucinatory crisis. The headline asks whether this avant-garde spy drama is worth the riddles, and the reviewer finds the riddles frustrating. So it's a mixed verdict, but a useful one. McCarthy is a writer who divides readers, and the real interest here is the argument about whether his method pays off or simply keeps the reader at a distance. If you enjoy thrillers, it's worth seeing how an experimental writer plays with the spy genre, even if the review suggests it may test your patience.

Bookmunch, meanwhile, has a review of Hermione Lee's biography Anita Brookner: Art and Life. The title of the review speaks of attempts to restore Brookner's reputation. The text I have is only that title, so I can't say much about the argument. But the pairing of art and life in the book's own title is a good fit for your interest in how painting and fiction speak to each other. Brookner was, after all, an art historian as well as a novelist, and a biography by Hermione Lee is likely to be careful, handsome and thoughtful.

Moving to history, migration and the stories that carry them. Literary Hub has an interview with Mary Beth Keane about Whale Harbor, her fifth novel. It follows the Irish diaspora from County Cork to Galveston in the nineteenth century. She also draws on her own family lineage, which gives the book a personal root as well as a historical one. This is exactly the kind of novel that can teach migration history from the inside, through particular people and particular crossings, rather than through dates and statistics. A route from Cork to Texas is not one most of us would think of straight away, so it could open up a corner of history that feels fresh.

Also on Literary Hub, there's an essay on how Derek Walcott's postcolonial epic helped a novelist write their own book. It places Walcott within the classical tradition, and it notes Luis Rafael Sánchez recasting Sophocles' Antigone in a fictional Caribbean republic. I love that detail. Antigone, with her defiance of the state in the name of the dead, travels very naturally into a postcolonial setting, and it's a nice example of how classical sources keep being reborn elsewhere. If you ever want to link the Greek tragedies to modern writing with your older pupils, this essay might offer a few good stepping stones.

Another Literary Hub essay, "The Ghostly and the Real", looks at how African literature treats the boundary between the living and the dead. Ancestors and spirits appear there as part of lived reality, rather than as something supernatural or added for effect. It's a useful corrective for readers who might otherwise file such scenes under "magic" or fantasy. It suggests that these novels teach culture and history from within, and that the dead are present in the story in the same way as anyone else.

Then there's the Southeast Review's assessment of Arundhati Roy's Mother Mary Comes to Me, her memoir of her mother. The text I have is thin, and the review's title is a line of dialogue, "This is Arundhati, my dear", which suggests something intimate and personal. I'd only say that a memoir of a formidable mother, written by a novelist known for her lyrical prose, is likely to be worth your attention, but I can't tell you more than that from what's in front of me.

Finally, language for its own sake. Backlisted has rerun its 2020 Hallowe'en episode on Beowulf. It's a long, lively conversation comparing translations by Seamus Heaney, Tolkien, Michael Morpurgo and Maria Dahvana Headley. What I enjoy about this is the sense that the poem has no single voice in English. Each translator has to decide how to carry its rhythm and strangeness into a modern language, and hearing them set side by side is a bit like comparing different performances of the same piece of music. It's a rerun, but since it was made for Hallowe'en, it's still seasonal enough, and it might be fun to dip into with a cup of something hot.

On the poetry side, Literary Hub's roundup of new poetry to read this November is led by Malgorzata Lebda's collection Mer de Glace, in Mira Rosenthal's translation. The opening lines quoted are lyrical, and the translator's notes are mentioned as part of the appeal. The title, Mer de Glace, is the name of the glacier above Chamonix, which is not so far from you, though I can't say from what I have whether the collection is set there. Still, a poetry collection with that title feels worth a look from anyone who lives with mountains on the horizon. The roundup's headline also mentions glass skulls, luminosity and soup, which is a rather wonderful range of subjects for a month of poems.

And last of all, a small atmospheric find. Literary Hub has a lyrical passage set on a bay at sunset, around Shep's Island, which seems to open a longer piece called "The Shared Life of Egan and Lucian". The text I have is thin, so I can't tell you what the piece is about, but the prose is atmospheric, and it may reward a few minutes of your time if you like writing that begins with light on water.

That's the literary round for today, and I hope something here keeps you company over your next coffee.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet couple of days at home, but there's a good deal of painting, photography and storytelling further afield, so let me start close to you and then travel.

In Grenoble, Le Pèlerin has a feature on the Tour Perret, describing it as a balcony on the Alps. I only have the headline and the framing, but if you enjoy the city's architecture and its place in local history, it looks like a pleasant read. Another local piece comes from l'Essentiel, about the Mistral district, where residents are telling the story of their own neighbourhood in their own words. The text is short, but it points to a project built on memory and voices, which you might enjoy for its own sake. One practical note from the Musée de Grenoble: several rooms are temporarily closed this autumn. The notice gives no dates and no details of which rooms, so it's worth checking before you plan a visit. And in the wider Isère, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that a Tim Burton exhibition in Bourgoin-Jallieu is proving a hit, with one visitor saying they've been a fan from the very beginning. All I have is the headline, so I can't tell you what the show contains, but it's clearly drawing the crowds.

Moving to Paris and the châteaux, Beaux Arts Magazine has two pieces. At the Fondation Cartier, Ibrahim Mahama and artists from the Ghanaian scene present a large exhibition imagining another future. It runs until February, so there's time. The text I have is cut short, but this is a substantial show by a leading contemporary artist. The other piece is more of a feast, quite literally. At the Château de Chambord, festive tables recreate four centuries of banquets, and each dish is meant as a bite-sized window into its period. It's history taught through food and objects, which is rather your territory: the sense that you learn an age by sitting at its table.

Now to Britain, where a few stories connect paintings with ideas in a way that would suit a classroom. The National Gallery has a video in which Yinka Shonibare explains how Gainsborough's Mr and Mrs Andrews inspired his reinterpretation, Mr and Mrs Andrews without their Heads. He talks through the thinking behind his choices, and the themes are class, power and identity. The two works are being shown together for the first time. It's a lovely example of one artist reading another across the centuries, and a way into how a painting can carry a whole social world.

At Tate St Ives, a retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham has opened, with her large Glacier, Blue Cave at its centre. The Guardian tells the story of an artist long sidelined in the history of St Ives, whose work was inspired by glaciers, by Vietnam, and by her own divorce. The headline promises beaches, Beatles and a broken marriage, which is a rather novelistic set of ingredients. At Tate Modern, there's a major survey of Ana Mendieta, whose work centres on the earth, the female body and her very distinctive practice. Hyperallergic calls it a strong piece of art history, and with a London show involved, it might be a good one to keep in mind for your British-section pupils.

On the photography side, The Guardian offers two picture galleries. Nicolas Rachline's book Elsebound has painterly, dreamlike images inspired by Edward Hopper and Blade Runner, and the artist explains how he developed his haunting style. Given your love of the links between painting and storytelling, the Hopper connection feels apt: those are pictures that seem to be waiting for a narrator. The second gallery is by Laura Pannack, who has won the inaugural Tom Stoddart award for Crossings, a project following young people in South Africa on their journeys to and from school. The photographs document the physical and psychological challenges of those journeys, and it's a sobering reminder of how much effort some young people put into simply getting to a classroom.

Finally, a few things for reading and listening. Hyperallergic has a roundup of ten art books to curl up with this November. The text is brief, but it mentions a Celia Paul essay collection written from Venice, a study of Salman Toor's painted worlds, and the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg. That last one is a wonderful mix of history, botany and a private life, and the whole list leans towards essays and writing about art, which suits you. Beaux Arts Magazine also has a short profile, Simone Fattal in two minutes. She was born in nineteen forty-two and has spent fifty years working across painting, sculpture and ceramics, so it's a concise introduction to a long career.

And on the radio, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has Grandmaster Flash, one of the founding fathers of hip-hop, talking about his life in music and his memoir, Birth of a Culture. There's also a segment on the cultural and literary significance of the Ramayana, as a new film appears. The programme also features Patrick Stewart, but the Ramayana discussion is likely the strand for you.

That's the round-up for today, Yamuna. I hope your day has a little light in it, perhaps with something painted, or something well told.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It is a quiet-ish couple of days in the art world, but there is a good deal to talk about, from your own corner of the Alps to Paris, London and a few pages worth curling up with.

Let me begin close to home, with a practical note. The Musée de Grenoble has put up a notice called "Un musée en mouvement", telling visitors that several rooms are temporarily closed this autumn. The excerpt gives no dates and no details about which rooms, so I can't tell you what is affected. If you are planning a visit, it is worth checking the museum's own pages first, so that the painting you are hoping to see is not behind a closed door.

Still in Grenoble, Le Pèlerin has run a feature on the Tour Perret, presenting it as a balcony on the Alps. It is a nice way of thinking about a building: not only as a landmark you glimpse from the tram, but as a place from which the whole ring of mountains is offered to you. I only have the framing of the piece, not its detail, but if you enjoy the city's architecture and its place in local history, it looks like a pleasant read, and it might send you back up there with fresh eyes.

There is also a small and rather lovely local story from l'Essentiel. In Grenoble, a project has the residents of the Mistral district telling the story of their neighbourhood in their own words. The text is brief, so I can't say what form it takes, but I like the idea very much. It is oral history, really: a place told by the people who live in it, rather than by the people who write about it. For someone who loves novels that teach history better than history essays, there is a kind of kinship there. Voices, memories and a sense of place do much of the work that plot would do in a book.

And a little further out in the Isère, at Bourgoin-Jallieu, an exhibition on Tim Burton is, according to Le Dauphiné Libéré, doing very well with visitors. The headline quotes one of them saying, "I've been a fan from the beginning." That is all I have, just the headline, so I can't tell you what is in the show. But it is a cheerful sign that a regional venue can draw a crowd, and it might be one to bear in mind if any of your pupils are Burton admirers.

Now, to Paris. Beaux Arts Magazine reports on a large exhibition at the Fondation Cartier, running until February, in which Ibrahim Mahama and artists from the Ghanaian scene imagine another future. The text I have is cut short, so I can't walk you through the rooms, but the premise is striking: a leading contemporary artist bringing a whole community of artists with him, and asking not what the past was, but what a different future might look like. It is a substantial show, and with a run until February, there is time to plan a trip.

Beaux Arts Magazine also offers a very short profile, "Simone Fattal en 2 minutes". Fattal was born in 1942 and has spent fifty years working across painting, sculpture and ceramics. It is a concise introduction to an artist whose work moves between materials, and the kind of quick portrait that leaves you wanting to know more. If you like the idea of an artist who has quietly built a lifetime of work, it is a pleasant two minutes.

And the same magazine takes us to the Château de Chambord, where festive tables recreate four centuries of feasting. Each dish is meant as a bite-sized window into a period, so that you taste the history rather than just read about it. I rather like this as a way into the past. A table is a surprisingly complete document: it tells you who was invited, what was valued, what was available, and how people wished to be seen. It is history through material culture, and it is not far from what a good novelist does when a meal on the page tells you everything about the people eating it.

From there, across the Channel, and to a pair of paintings in conversation. The National Gallery has released a video in which Yinka Shonibare explains how Gainsborough's "Mr and Mrs Andrews" inspired his own reinterpretation, "Mr and Mrs Andrews without their Heads". He talks through the thinking behind his choices, and the video takes up questions of class, power and identity. What makes it especially interesting is that the two works are being shown together for the first time. For a teacher of English literature, this is a gift. Gainsborough's couple, posed with their land behind them, are a portrait of ownership and social standing, and Shonibare's version asks what happens when you take away the faces and look at what remains: the clothes, the stance, the property, the assumptions. It is a very good example of how an artist can read an old image the way a critic reads a text, or the way a novelist rewrites a classic from a different point of view. I can imagine it working well with older pupils, as a way into ideas about reading, adaptation and who gets to be seen.

Also in Britain, a retrospective of the modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham has opened at Tate St Ives. The Guardian describes how she has become a radical art icon, and its piece is titled with beaches, Beatles and a broken marriage. At the centre of the show is her large work "Glacier (Blue Cave)". She is an artist who was long sidelined from the art history of St Ives, and the piece explores how her work drew on glaciers, on Vietnam and on her own divorce. I find that combination quite moving: the vast, slow, frozen scale of a glacier set against the private upheaval of a marriage ending. It is also a reminder of how often the story of a place gets told around certain names, while others wait decades to be properly looked at. Since you live under the Belledonne range, a painter so taken by ice and mountains might appeal to you in particular.

Then Tate Modern, where a major survey revisits the work of Ana Mendieta. Hyperallergic has a piece called "Ana Mendieta's Lasting Imprint on Art", and describes her work as centred on the earth, the female body and her own distinctive practice. The writer treats it as a strong piece of art history, and it seems to me it would suit a British-section teacher well, since the show is in London and the questions it raises, about body, landscape and presence, are rich ones to bring to a classroom. Mendieta's work is also a good example of art that leaves a mark rather than an object, and the word "imprint" in the title is well chosen.

Now to photography, where two stories sit side by side in The Guardian. The first is Nicolas Rachline's book "Elsebound", whose painterly, dreamlike images are inspired by Edward Hopper and by Blade Runner. The Guardian presents the pictures, and the artist explains how he developed his haunting style. There is something wonderful about that pairing. Hopper gave us solitary figures in lit windows and empty diners; Blade Runner gave us rain, neon and uncertainty. Put the two together and you have a very particular mood, strangely quiet and slightly unreal, that sits somewhere between a painting and a film still. The headline mentions clowns, so there is a touch of the uncanny too. It is a good example of what you like: an image world that has clearly been shaped by earlier paintings.

The second is a more grounded story. Laura Pannack has won the inaugural Tom Stoddart award for her project "Crossings", which follows young people in South Africa on their journeys to and from school. The photographs document the physical and psychological challenges of those journeys. I like that the subject is so ordinary and so enormous at the same time. A walk to school is something we hardly think about, and here it becomes a way of understanding how a young person experiences their country, their effort and their hopes. Since you teach teenagers, it may be a moving set of pictures to look at.

And finally, a few things for the reading chair. Hyperallergic has a roundup called "10 Art Books to Curl Up With This November". The text is brief, but it mentions a collection of essays by Celia Paul written from Venice, a study of Salman Toor's painted worlds, and the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg. I think that last one is a particularly lovely idea: a revolutionary thinker who also pressed and kept plants, a private, patient, tender side of someone remembered for public fire. With the essays and the history together, it is a list that suits a reader who likes art linked to writing, and it arrives just as the evenings are drawing in.

And on the radio, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has Grandmaster Flash, one of the founding fathers of hip-hop, talking about his life in music and his memoir "Birth of a Culture". The programme also includes a segment on the cultural and literary significance of the Ramayana, as a new film appears. That second strand may be the one for you, since it is about a story that has shaped literature and imagination for a very long time. The programme also features Patrick Stewart, in case that is of interest.

That is the round-up for today, Yamuna. I hope something in it sends you off to a gallery, a bookshop or a high viewpoint over the valley, with a good cup of something warm afterwards.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Hamlet-heavy couple of days in the BFI corner, with Orwell close behind and a few useful ideas for Twelfth Night and for teaching Shakespeare to younger pupils.

Let's start with Hamlet, which is on the 2027 programme and seems to be turning up everywhere. The most talked-about piece of news is a stage production called Hamlet Hail to the Thief, which fuses Shakespeare's play with the music of Radiohead. London Theatre has an interview with its co-director, Steven Hoggett, about how the two worlds are brought together. Matinee Musicals reports that the production is beginning its London run at the Barbican, and Broadway Shows, in a November roundup of London theatre, lists a Radiohead-scored Hamlet alongside a production of Nero and a Sondheim celebration. I should be honest that for those last two, only the headlines came through, so I can't tell you more about the staging. But the Hoggett interview is the one to look at if you're thinking about adaptation. A contemporary musical reworking would make a lively comparison for première pupils: what does a song do to a soliloquy, and what is lost or gained when Hamlet's language is carried by music instead?

Music of a very different kind comes from Planet Hugill, which reviews Chelsea Opera Group's performance of Ambroise Thomas's opera Hamlet. Jacques Imbrailo sings the prince and Haegee Lee is Ophélie, under the direction of Jonathon Cole-Swinard, whom the reviewer calls sympathetic. The headline says "Forget Shakespeare", which is a provocative way of saying that the opera deserves attention in its own right. Given your love of classical music, this one may appeal beyond the classroom, and it's a nice reminder that Ophelia, in particular, gets rather different treatment once she has a French name and a voice to sing with.

Further afield, Newstrack English offers an analysis of Haider, Vishal Bhardwaj's film that reimagines Hamlet in Kashmir. It looks at how the story is carried into a new political and cultural landscape. This is a very good lens for teaching adaptation, because it asks pupils what is essential in Hamlet once Denmark has gone. And for something quieter, The Quill has a review of David Wroblewski's novel The Story of Edgar Sawtelle, a family tragedy on a Wisconsin dog farm that echoes Hamlet. Only the title came through in the text, so I can't say much about the review itself, but a novel with a Hamlet shadow and a farm setting might be one to keep in mind for the narrator-driven fiction you enjoy.

Staying with directors, Plays International reviews Elizabeth Schafer and David Bullen's Arden study, Shakespeare in the Theatre: Phyllida Lloyd. It looks at how one director has interpreted Shakespeare on stage, and it should be useful for teaching both Twelfth Night and Hamlet through stage practice rather than through the page alone. On the same theme, The Times Gazette reports that SSCC Theatre is opening an Edwardian-era staging of Twelfth Night. A period setting like that is a neat way to ask pupils how a production reframes the social world of the play: what happens to Malvolio, or to Viola's disguise, when the clothes and manners belong to a different England?

Now to Orwell. 1984 is on the oral-themes list, and there's a cluster of coverage of a new production at the Royal Lyceum in Edinburgh. Everything Theatre has a review, and Fife Today gives it four stars, calling it a challenging watch and a powerful recreation of Orwell's novel. I only have the headlines and short summaries, so I can't tell you how the staging handles the text, but the verdict is strong enough that it may be worth seeing if you're in Britain, or worth discussing with pupils through the reviews. In a more heartening vein, the Belleville News-Democrat reports that students at Rock Valley College have staged 1984. The article is brief, but it is nice to see young people tackling the novel on stage, and it might give your pupils a sense that this is a text people really do perform and argue over.

A related idea comes from Plays International, which covers The Lives of Others at the Adelphi Theatre, the stage version of the film about surveillance in East Germany. Its theme of Stasi watching connects naturally with 1984, and the two together could anchor a good class discussion on state surveillance, and on how fiction makes watching feel intimate and frightening.

For teaching younger pupils, The Guardian marks thirty years of Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet with a feature on how it made teenagers fall in love with Shakespeare. Only the headline reached me, but the angle is a useful one for seconde: what draws a teenager to Shakespeare in the first place? Theatre Weekly also reports that Shakespeare's Globe has announced A Midsummer Night's Dream for 2027, as part of its Playing Shakespeare with Deutsche Bank season. There are no dates or cast in the text I have, so it's one to watch for further details.

Finally, a thought for the more reflective moments. Blue News has a short interview with the filmmaker Raoul Peck, who says, "Art without a purpose is not art." It's brief, but it touches on documentary and artistic commitment, and it might sit nicely beside the Orwell and surveillance material as a prompt about what writers and artists are for.

That's all for today, Yamuna, and I hope your Tuesday has a little more Shakespeare than surveillance in it.

So the production is clearly one of the month's talking points.

What makes this useful for you is the question of adaptation. When a director sets a play to a rock band's music, what is being claimed about Hamlet? Perhaps that his restlessness, his grief and his sense of a rotten world are feelings that music can carry as well as verse can. Your première students might enjoy being asked a simple question: if you were scoring Hamlet, which moments would you give to music, and which would you leave to silence, or to the language alone? Hoggett's interview is worth a look in advance, because directors talking about why they made a choice are often more convincing to teenagers than critics explaining it afterwards.

Hamlet has also turned up this week in an opera house. Planet Hugill reviews Chelsea Opera Group's performance of Ambroise Thomas's opera Hamlet, with Jacques Imbrailo in the title role and Haegee Lee as Ophélie, under the conductor Jonathon Cole-Swinard. The review's headline says "Forget Shakespeare", which is a provocative thing to say about a Hamlet, and the argument is that Thomas's opera makes a strong case for itself and deserves attention in its own right. I'd take that with a smile, of course, but it's a lovely reminder that the play has been retold in many art forms, and given your fondness for classical music, it may be a pleasure to read for its own sake. For class, it raises a nice point: what does a character gain, and what does she lose, when she must sing rather than speak? The French spelling of Ophélie in the title reminds us that the story crossed the Channel and came back changed, which suits your bilingual setting rather well.

Another Hamlet, further afield, is Haider. Newstrack English has an analysis of how Vishal Bhardwaj reimagined Hamlet in Kashmir. Here the play is lifted out of Elsinore and set in a place where politics, family loyalty and suspicion are fused in a very different way. This is the sort of adaptation that rewards students who already know the original, because they can watch the structure of the play survive while its world is entirely transformed. It's a good way into the question of what in Hamlet is universal and what is bound to its setting, and it speaks to your wish for stories that can be entered without already knowing the culture. I'd suggest it as a reading for you before it becomes anything for the classroom, as the analysis may help you decide which scenes to compare.

There's one more Hamlet echo, this time in a novel. The Quill has a review of David Wroblewski's The Story of Edgar Sawtelle, a family tragedy on a Wisconsin dog farm that echoes Hamlet. I only have the title and the short description here, so I can't tell you much about the review itself. But the premise is intriguing, and given how much you value strong narrators and novels that borrow from older works, it may be one for your own reading shelf, or for a student who finishes the play and asks what to read next.

Staying with Shakespeare in performance, Plays International reviews a new Arden Shakespeare study, Shakespeare in the Theatre: Phyllida Lloyd, by Elizabeth Schafer and David Bullen. It looks at the director's Shakespeare productions, and the reviewer's interest is in how a director interprets the plays. This is relevant to both Twelfth Night and Hamlet on the twenty twenty-seven list. For teaching, the value of a book like this is that it treats each production as an argument about the text. It could give you a framework for asking students not "what does the play mean?" but "what has this director decided it means, and how can you tell from the staging?" That is a very good habit for the oral and for the written commentary.

On Twelfth Night, there's a small but interesting item from The Times Gazette. SSCC Theatre is opening an Edwardian-era staging of the play. The text gives only the period setting, but that alone is enough to start a discussion. An Edwardian world is one of strict class, careful manners and social ladders, and so it throws into relief the play's themes of disguise, status and mistaken identity. Malvolio's ambitions, Viola's disguise as a young man, and Olivia's household all take on a particular flavour when dressed in that period. A good classroom question might be: what does a setting emphasise and what does it hide? You could ask students to choose their own era for the play and justify it from the text.

Now to Orwell, whose Nineteen Eighty-Four is one of the oral themes, and which seems to be having a busy week on stage in Edinburgh. The Royal Lyceum is staging it, and two reviews have appeared. Everything Theatre has a review of the production, and Fife Today gives it four stars, calling it a challenging watch and a powerful recreation of Orwell's novel. I don't have more detail than that, so I can't tell you about the staging choices, but the verdict is a strong one, and the phrase "challenging watch" is telling. It suggests a production that doesn't let its audience off lightly, which is rather the point of the book.

For your students, reviews like these are useful because they show a text working in performance. A novel that happens largely inside one man's head, with surveillance and the manipulation of language at its heart, must find a way to be seen. How do you stage a thought? How do you stage a telescreen? Even without the production details, you could invite students to imagine solutions and then compare them with what the reviewers describe when you read the two pieces together. It's also a fine exercise in critical writing, since the two reviews, one star-rated and one not, give you two different ways of judging a performance.

A much humbler staging is nevertheless worth a mention. The Belleville News-Democrat reports that students at Rock Valley College have brought Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four to the stage. The text is brief, but it's a heartening little story, young people choosing to wrestle with this book and perform it. If you ever want to nudge your own students towards a reading, a performance or a drama club project, it's a nice example to share. It also shows that this novel still draws people in who are close in age to your pupils.

A related idea comes from Plays International, which has a piece on The Lives of Others at the Adelphi Theatre. This is the stage version of the film about surveillance in East Germany. The Stasi theme is a natural companion to Orwell, since both works are about what happens when the state watches its citizens and when private life becomes a danger. I'd be cautious about claiming more than the headline and summary tell us, but as a pairing it's rich. You might ask students how the two works treat the person who watches as well as the person who is watched, and whether fiction about real regimes changes how we read fiction about imagined ones. It could make a strong comparative discussion for the oral, especially as it links history, which you love, with literature.

On a lighter and wider note, The Guardian marks thirty years of Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet, with a feature on how it made teenagers fall in love with Shakespeare. Again I only have the headline, so I can't give you the arguments, but the angle is a useful one for your seconde classes. It raises the question of what gets young people through the door with Shakespeare: spectacle, music, modern dress, or simply being treated as capable of understanding it. It may be a nice companion to the Radiohead Hamlet conversation, because both are bets that Shakespeare can speak through a contemporary idiom.

Also on the Shakespeare front, Theatre Weekly reports that Shakespeare's Globe has announced A Midsummer Night's Dream for twenty twenty-seven, as part of its Playing Shakespeare with Deutsche Bank season. There are no dates or cast in the text, so it's one to watch rather than plan around. It's not on the programme, but it might interest you as a possible outing or a talking point with younger students.

Finally, something a little different. Blue News has an interview with the filmmaker Raoul Peck, in which he argues that art without a purpose is not art. The text is short, but the remark touches on documentary and artistic commitment, and I thought it might appeal to you. It's a provocative line to put in front of older students, perhaps in première or the new terminale group. Does a work need a purpose to count as art? Is Orwell's purpose part of his art, or does the art survive without it? Does Hamlet have a purpose? It's a good, slightly mischievous debate starter, and it connects neatly to the surveillance and adaptation threads running through everything else today.

If I had to pick a few things to take away, I'd say the Hoggett interview and the Haider analysis for Hamlet, the pair of Edinburgh reviews for Nineteen Eighty-Four, and the Phyllida Lloyd review as a way of thinking about directing. Everything else is lovely background, and a few pieces are thin on detail, so I'd read them as signposts rather than sources.

That's the corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope the day's reading finds you with a warm drink and a bit of quiet.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet, early-November stretch in the valley, with a handful of evenings out coming up and a good run of exhibitions that will keep you busy well into the winter.

Let me start with the nearest thing, which is tonight. Tuesday the third of November, at half past eight, the film club at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage is showing Sidney Lumet's The Verdict. It's a courtroom drama built around a memorable central character, so it's close to the sort of fiction you like, and it's a short hop from Les Adrets if you fancy a film on a weeknight.

Then, looking ahead, there's music. On Sunday the eighth of November, Vizille hosts a concert pairing organ and violin, as Le Dauphiné Libéré announces. The report is brief, so I can't tell you the programme or the time, but organ and violin in a village setting sounds like a lovely classical evening, and Vizille is not far from Grenoble. Worth a quick look at the details if it tempts you.

Over at Hexagone, the Scène nationale in Meylan, there are two pieces in the coming week. On Friday the sixth of November at ten in the morning, the company En Cie d'Eux performs T·R·U·C, an object-theatre show that mixes theatre, music and dance. It's for children aged five and up, runs fifty minutes, and has three more dates listed, so if you know any young people who might enjoy it, there's flexibility. Then on Tuesday the tenth of November at eight in the evening, the company Frag presents Faire troupeau, in French, a blend of theatre and documentary. It's described as a joyful odyssey about the power of the collective, and it runs one hour twenty. That one may appeal to you as an evening of storytelling with a real-life edge.

A little further off, but worth pencilling in, is the circus. From the twenty-fourth to the twenty-seventh of November, MC2 in Grenoble presents Qui som?, a family show by Baro d'evel. It's a physical, theatrical piece, and the run of several days gives you room to choose a convenient evening or weekend slot. And just beyond your usual radius, on Saturday the fourteenth of November in Autrans-Méaudre-en-Vercors, a former resident is organising a concert in the village. Le Dauphiné Libéré gives little detail, but it's the sort of small, local gathering that can turn out to be rather charming.

Now to the exhibitions, where there's a good deal on offer, and nothing is rushed because most of them run for months.

In Grenoble, the free exhibition Anne Truitt, Libérer la couleur runs from the third of October until the tenth of January. It's a show about colour, and I think it's the one most likely to set off those conversations between painting and writing that you enjoy. Colour as something you almost read, rather than simply look at, might make a nice thread for a class, too.

Also in Grenoble, and also free, is Drowning World, a photography exhibition by Gideon Mendel, open until the twenty-fifth of April next year. The notice is short, but the title and the photographer's name suggest something serious and image-led, and the long run means you can choose a quiet afternoon.

Another Grenoble show with a long life is De tous bois, devoted to the Hache family of cabinetmakers and to contemporary design. It's free and runs until the twenty-fifth of April 2027. It sets fine woodworking beside new creative work, which makes it a pleasant choice for a weekend if you like craft and the stories objects can tell.

And then there is Encordés, which follows the pioneering mountain guides. It opened on the fifteenth of October and runs until the twenty-seventh of February. The description is brief, but it speaks directly to the landscape of Belledonne above your house, and to the history of the people who first learned to move through it. If you like history told through place rather than through dates, this could be a good one.

Closer to home, in Allevard, the exhibition Électrique ! Les Forges d'Allevard à l'assaut de la Houille blanche is free and runs until the third of January. It tells the story of the Forges d'Allevard and the rise of hydroelectric power, the so-called white coal, in the Isère. It's industrial history, but history rooted in the valley you live in, told through materials and landscape, and Allevard is an easy outing from the Adrets.

One small note on something you've just missed. Yesterday afternoon, Grenoble's Saint-Laurent archaeological museum offered a free guided visit. That's gone now, but it's a reminder that the museum, with the city's buried past, is worth a visit of your own when you have a free hour.

Finally, a few pieces of local life and landscape. Le Dauphiné Libéré has published photographs from weather stations around Grenoble showing the sea of cloud filling the valleys. You'll know the view from Les Adrets, and the pictures look striking, so they're worth a glance on your phone with a coffee. The same paper has a piece on Créa'Léna, a Grésivaudan initiative that aims to spread positive messages about young people. Only the headline is available, so I can't say more, but it's a cheerful local story, and perhaps one that would resonate with your work. And Grenoble Mag reports that Coublevie, near Voiron, has four events planned to enliven the end of the year. There are no dates or details yet, but if you like village life, it may be worth keeping an eye out for more.

So, a film tonight if you feel like it, music and theatre next week, and plenty of time to wander through the exhibitions at your own pace; I hope you find something to enjoy.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Tuesday the third of November, and this briefing gathers what's on around you, from a film tonight in the valley to exhibitions in Grenoble that will keep you busy well into the new year.

Let me start with the evenings, beginning with tonight. At half past eight, at the Centre Culturel Jeannine Creissels, known as Le Belvédère, in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage, the Ciné-club du Belvédère is showing Sidney Lumet's The Verdict. It's a courtroom drama with a strong, memorable central character, which puts it close to the kind of fiction you love. Courtroom stories tend to work like good novels, because everything depends on voices, on who is telling the truth and how well they tell it. The listing comes through the Grésivaudan agenda. If you're not too tired after a day of teaching, it could be a good way to spend a Tuesday evening, and you'd be home before it gets too late.

Next, a classical evening a little further off. On Sunday the eighth of November, in Vizille, there is a concert pairing organ and violin, announced by Le Dauphiné Libéré. The announcement is short, and I don't have the time, the venue or the programme, so you'd want to check those before setting out. But organ and violin is a lovely combination, one instrument vast and architectural, the other singing and close to the human voice. Vizille is an easy run from Grenoble, and a Sunday concert there would suit a quiet autumn weekend.

Staying with the stage, Hexagone, the Scène nationale in Meylan, has two things in the coming days. The first is for younger audiences. On Friday the sixth of November at ten in the morning, the company En Cie d'Eux performs T, R, U, C, an object-theatre show that mixes theatre, music and dance, for children aged five and up. It lasts fifty minutes, and there are three more dates listed. It's a gentle family option close to home, so keep it in mind if there are nieces, nephews or friends' children around. And since it plays at ten in the morning, it may also suit a school group.

The second is for adults. On Tuesday the tenth of November at eight in the evening, again at Hexagone in Meylan, the company Frag presents Faire troupeau, a French-language piece that blends theatre and documentary. The programme text calls it a joyful odyssey about the power of the collective. It runs an hour and twenty minutes. I like the idea of an odyssey in the title, with its echo of old storytelling, applied to something as ordinary and as important as people acting together. Theatre that borrows the methods of documentary can be very moving, because the stories are real but the telling is shaped, almost like fiction.

Now to something that falls a little later in the month, but is worth noting early. From the twenty-fourth to the twenty-seventh of November, at the MC2 in Grenoble, the company Baro d'evel presents Qui som?, a family circus show. It's a live performance with a physical, theatrical quality, and it could make a good weekend outing, with a few weeks to plan.

Turning to exhibitions, Grenoble has a very rich selection at the moment, and most of them run for months, so there's no pressure to go this week. Let me take them one at a time.

First, Anne Truitt, Libérer la couleur, which means freeing colour. It's free, in Grenoble, and runs from the third of October until the tenth of January. It's a show about colour, the kind of visual art that invites the links to literature that you enjoy. I can't tell you more about what's on the walls from the listing, but a show built around colour can be a good prompt for thinking about how writers use it, the way a single colour in a paragraph can carry a whole mood. If you ever want a fresh angle for a class on description or imagery, an afternoon there might give you one.

Second, Encordés, dans les pas des guides pionniers, or roped together, in the footsteps of the pioneering guides. It's in Grenoble, from the fifteenth of October until the twenty-seventh of February. The listing is brief, but the subject speaks directly to the mountains you live in, and to the local history of the people who first made them accessible. Living in Les Adrets, with Belledonne above you, you'll have your own sense of those slopes, and it may be interesting to see them through the story of those who first roped up and went. There's a long run, so it's an easy one to fit in on a grey winter Saturday.

Third, De tous bois, a free exhibition in Grenoble on the Hache cabinetmakers and contemporary design. It runs right until the twenty-fifth of April next year. It pairs fine woodworking with new creative work, so you see the craft of the past alongside what designers are doing now. It's a good pick for a craft-minded weekend, and the long run means you can visit whenever the mood takes you.

Fourth, a photography exhibition, Drowning World, by Gideon Mendel. It's free, in Grenoble, and also runs until the twenty-fifth of April. The listing is short, but the title and the photographer's name suggest a serious, image-led show. I'd say go in knowing it may be a sober hour rather than a light one, but photography can say things in a single frame that pages of prose struggle to.

And a fifth Grenoble suggestion, though this one has already passed. Yesterday, the second of November, at half past two in the afternoon, there was a free guided visit of the Saint-Laurent archaeological museum. I mention it because it's a good fit for a history-minded visitor, and the museum itself is a place to see the city's buried past up close. The listing only covered that one afternoon, so if you missed it, I'd suggest checking the museum's own schedule for another time.

One more exhibition, this one up in the Belledonne foothills. At Allevard, from the first of April until the third of January, there is a free exhibition called Électrique! Les Forges d'Allevard à l'assaut de la Houille blanche. It tells the story of the Forges d'Allevard and the rise of hydroelectric power, the so-called white coal, in the Isère. White coal is a wonderful phrase, by the way, the power of falling water named as if it were a mineral. It's industrial history told through material and place, in a valley you know. With a closing date just after the new year, it's the one of these exhibitions with the nearest deadline, so if it appeals, I'd plan it for the coming weeks rather than leaving it. Allevard is also a pleasant place to wander on its own, so it could be an easy half day.

Now a few pieces about local life and the landscape. Le Dauphiné Libéré has published a set of photographs from weather stations around Grenoble, showing the sea of cloud filling the valleys. It's a visually striking piece, and a view you may know from your own window in Les Adrets, looking down over the Grésivaudan. On mornings when the valley disappears under that white layer and the peaks stand out above it, it feels like a painting waiting for a caption. If the cloud is low where you are today, it's worth a look at the photographs, and perhaps a walk upward to get above it yourself.

Also from Le Dauphiné Libéré, a piece on Créa'Léna, an initiative in the Grésivaudan that aims to send positive messages about young people. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you more about how it works. But the subject is local and upbeat, and as someone who spends her days with teenagers, you may find it speaks to you.

Then Grenoble Mag reports that in Coublevie, near Voiron, four events are planned to liven up the end of the year. The article as I have it doesn't give dates or details, so it's more a pointer than a plan. Still, it's the kind of village life, with small gatherings as the year winds down, that is often well worth a detour, and it's within reach of Les Adrets if the programme turns out to suit you.

And finally, a small cultural event just beyond our usual area. On Saturday the fourteenth of November, in Autrans-Méaudre-en-Vercors, a former resident is organising a concert in the village, according to Le Dauphiné Libéré. The text is brief, so I can't say what music will be played or where exactly. But there is something appealing about a concert organised by someone who has come back to the place she once lived, and the Vercors in November has its own quiet beauty. It's a bit further than the usual radius, so it would be a proper outing rather than a quick trip.

To pull this together into a possible fortnight: tonight, The Verdict in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage. On Sunday the eighth, organ and violin in Vizille. On Tuesday the tenth, Faire troupeau in Meylan. At some point, an afternoon in Grenoble for Anne Truitt, and another for the mountain guides of Encordés. And on the quieter days, the long exhibitions in Allevard, Grenoble and Meylan are there waiting, with Allevard the one to see before the new year.

Whatever you choose, I hope there's a good sea of cloud to look down on from the house, and a story waiting at the end of the day.

france.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Tuesday the third of November, and today's France briefing has a literary prize, a busy week in the lycées, some hopeful news from the health service, and a probe on its way to an asteroid.

Let's begin with books, since the day has one worth watching. The Goncourt jury chooses its 2026 winner at a quarter to one this afternoon in Paris, franceinfo reports. Four novels remain on the shortlist, by Jaenada, Haenel, Mélois and Prudhomme. The winner will succeed Laurent Mauvignier, whose novel "La Maison vide" took last year's prize. If you're curious, the announcement should land just after lunch, in time for the shelves in every bookshop to be rearranged by teatime.

On the lighter side of language, The Local France has two pieces for a teacher's ear. The word of the day is "cauchemardesque", meaning nightmarish, offered to anyone who wants a little theatrical drama in their complaints. It's a lovely, rolling word, and I can imagine it going down well with a class of première pupils describing their Monday mornings. The expression of the day is "vis-à-vis", which turns up in everyday conversation, in the workplace, in the news and even in property listings, and has a wider range of uses than its English cousin. It might make a small, useful warm-up for a lesson.

Now to schools, where things are less calm. After two weeks of holidays, lycée pupils across France resumed their mobilisation today. The Local France says the blockades have restarted, with student leaders arguing that the government's proposals don't go far enough. Franceinfo adds that some schools are trying to combine protest with resumed lessons. Several pupils say they are anxious about what all this disruption means for their baccalauréat preparation, and one is quoted as saying he is very stressed about the bac. On the government side, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu repeats that he's ready to meet student representatives next week.

The anxiety is not confined to lycées. Éric Berton, president of Aix-Marseille University, warns that student mental health is getting worse in the face of the blockades, and that university support services are overloaded. He's asking the government to invest more in public higher education. It's a sober piece, but a reminder that behind the headlines there are young people who need looking after.

One more item for those who choose classroom resources. Franceinfo reports that the Île-de-France region apparently still offers digital school textbooks very similar to its withdrawn "manuels libres", despite a court ruling requiring their removal. Private publishers are complaining about it, so it's one to watch if you follow how teaching materials get chosen.

Turning to health, and to some encouraging news. From this week, almost three thousand "docteurs juniors" are starting their final year of medical training in the field. Both franceinfo and The Local France cover the story. They'll work with growing autonomy in practices and health centres, and they are mainly heading for areas short of GPs, many of them in rural France. The hope is simple: that patients can get appointments a little more easily, with, as one headline puts it, slightly shorter waiting times. After years of talk about medical deserts, it's a practical step, and one that may matter in the countryside.

There is also a programme tonight that might interest you. At five past nine on France 5, "Enquête de santé" broadcasts "Migraine, la fin du casse-tête ?". It follows a pioneering clinical trial at the university hospital in Clermont-Ferrand, described as unique in the world, which is raising real hopes for the roughly eleven million people in France who live with migraine. And a gentle reminder from the calendar: the Mois sans tabac began on Sunday, now in its eleventh edition and running through November. Professor Yves Martinet says that stopping smoking for a month multiplies by five the chances of quitting for good, which is a rather encouraging statistic for anyone who has been thinking about it.

Now, a story to lift the eyes upward. French astronaut Sophie Adenot has held her first press conference since completing a three-week fitness and readaptation programme at the European astronaut centre in Cologne. It's a warm story about a safe return from space, and about the slow business of getting used to gravity again.

And there's more from the sky tomorrow. On Wednesday the fourth of November, the Hera probe reaches the asteroid system that was the target of NASA's DART probe, which was deliberately crashed into an asteroid in 2022. Hera's task is to examine the damage, and in particular to answer the question franceinfo puts so neatly: did the impact produce a crater? It's the first test of its kind of defending a planet, and there's something rather wonderful about a spacecraft sent to inspect the scene of a deliberate collision.

Finally, La Mire, the daily zapping of French television, from the second of November. This edition touches on fuel prices, a renewed Trump threat against Iran, and an Ardèche craftsman who benefits from lower prices at the pump. The best detail, though, is from the New York Halloween parade, where one hundred and sixty-five zombies danced to Thriller. The summary I have is cut short, so I can't tell you what else the bulletin holds, but that image alone is worth the click.

That's the news for this morning, Yamuna, and I hope your day is more "charmant" than "cauchemardesque".
france.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Tuesday the third of November, and today's French news has a literary prize, a few new words, a school year already restless, some hopeful health stories, and a pleasing scattering of space.

Let me begin with books, since today is a big day for them. The Goncourt jury meets in Paris and, from a quarter to one this afternoon, will choose its 2026 winner. According to franceinfo, four novels remain in contention: those by Jaenada, Haenel, Mélois and Prudhomme. Whoever wins will succeed Laurent Mauvignier, whose novel "La Maison vide" took last year's prize. I only have the surnames and not the titles, but the announcement is at lunchtime, so by the time you're settling into your afternoon you may well know which of the four has taken it. It's always a fine moment for a teacher of fiction, because the winner so often ends up on someone's reading list, and perhaps on a few of your pupils' wish lists too.

Staying with language, The Local France has two small pieces for people who enjoy words. The first is the French Word of the Day, "cauchemardesque", meaning nightmarish. The Local suggests it's just the thing if you'd like to add a little theatrical drama to your complaints, and I rather like that. A dreadful commute is no longer merely unpleasant; it's cauchemardesque. The second is the Expression of the Day, "vis-à-vis". Anyone who has taught English to French speakers will know the false comfort of a word that looks the same in both languages. The Local points out that in French, vis-à-vis turns up everywhere: in everyday conversation, in workplace talk, in the political news, even in property listings. Its range is wider than the English equivalent. It's a handy reminder that the borrowed word often has a rather fuller life at home than abroad.

Now to schools, where the news is busier. Lycée pupils went back after two weeks of holidays, and the mobilisation that was under way before the break has picked up again. The Local France reports that high school blockades have restarted, with student leaders saying the government's proposals do not go far enough. Franceinfo adds that several school and student organisations are continuing the movement. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has repeated that he is ready to meet student representatives next week. Franceinfo also notes that in some schools the protest and the lessons are being combined, so that classes resume while the mobilisation carries on alongside them. It isn't a uniform picture across the country, then, and I imagine it will look a little different from one school to the next.

There's a human side to this that franceinfo brings out well. Some pupils are worried. One of them is quoted saying, "Je suis très stressé par le bac", meaning they're very stressed about the baccalauréat. Several students say they're anxious about how the disruption might affect their preparation for the exam. If you have première pupils, you'll know that the bac looms in everyone's mind long before it arrives, so I can well imagine that anxiety being quite close to the surface in your classroom this week.

Higher education has its own version of the same strain. Franceinfo reports that Éric Berton, the president of Aix-Marseille University, is warning about the worsening mental health of students in the face of the blockades. He says that the university's support services are overloaded, and he's asking the government to invest more in public higher education. It's a sober piece, and a reminder that behind the disruption there are young people who are tired, unsettled, and sometimes struggling.

One more item for those who choose teaching resources. Franceinfo says that the Île-de-France region reportedly still offers digital school textbooks very similar to its withdrawn "manuels libres", even though a court ruling required their removal. Private publishers are complaining about it. I don't have the details of how the region responds, but it matters to teachers who are deciding what to put in front of their classes.

Let me turn to health, where there's rather more good news. Beginning this week, around three thousand "docteurs juniors" are starting their final year of training out in the field. Franceinfo explains that they work with growing autonomy in practices and health centres, and The Local France puts the figure at almost three thousand young doctors taking up posts. They're going mainly to areas short of GPs, many of them in rural France, the so-called medical deserts. The hope is that patients will find it easier to get an appointment, and franceinfo quotes the phrase "des délais un peu moins longs", meaning waiting times a little shorter. It's a modest phrase, and honestly rather an honest one. Nobody is promising miracles, but anyone who lives in the hills and has ever tried to find a doctor will understand why it matters. For people in places like the Belledonne foothills, it's the sort of change that's worth watching.

There's more encouraging news on the medical front. Good morning, Yamuna. It is Tuesday the third of November, and the last two days have brought a kind collection of stories: islands switching off their lights for birds, a young violinist with a poet's touch, and a dog who would not let a sleeper rest.

A whole community simply agreed to sit in the dark for a few nights, and the birds went on their way.

Thirteen years of persistence are quietly folded into that one sentence, and I find that rather moving.

And from the ground we go up to the sky. The Optimist Daily also reports that astronomers have identified what is described as the first green star, and the article links it to chemistry left behind by a dead planet. I will not pretend to know more than that, but the picture is wonderful: a green star in the night sky, shaped by the remains of a world that no longer exists. It sounds like the opening line of a novel, and I suspect you could pass it to a seconde class as a writing prompt. What would a narrator say, looking up at it?

Now to art and music, which I hope will be especially welcome. At Tate St Ives, a retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham has opened. It is the kind of thing that is worth a minute and a half with a cup of coffee, and it tends to improve the rest of the morning.

Next, stories and young voices. Upworthy shares a rather touching item. A Japanese man has published his sister's diary from nineteen ninety-eight, when she was sixteen and spending a year as a foreign exchange student in Iowa. What comes through in the extract is a distinctive, observant young narrator, and in particular a quiet detail about waving to strangers on the road. That small custom, strangers waving to one another from the road, strikes her as worth recording, and the diary captures it with a freshness that only comes from seeing a place for the first time. It reads, I think, like the beginning of a coming-of-age story. Staying with care, though of a different kind, Positive News describes a new series of all-female fight nights. The fights themselves become a way of funding that, and a community gathers around it.

That brings us to ordinary kindness, which today arrives in two dramatic forms. The second is from Texas, again from Good News Network. Four men ran toward a fire on a highway to pull an eighteen-year-old from her burning car. One of them, Mike Argote, was burned in the effort. It reminds me of the kind of scene a novelist might linger over, a family at a long table, finally looking at one another.

So, from dark islands and green stars to a violinist's Tchaikovsky and a dog at the bedside, I hope the day treats you as gently as these stories treat their readers.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Tuesday, the third of November.

Let's start with a literary moment happening today. At a quarter to one in Paris, the Goncourt jury names its 2026 winner, according to franceinfo. Four novels are in the running: those by Jaenada, Haenel, Mélois and Prudhomme. Whoever wins will succeed Laurent Mauvignier, who took the prize last year with La Maison vide. It might be worth keeping your phone nearby over lunch.

Staying with books, there is a good handful this morning. Bookmunch has a review of Hermione Lee's new biography, Anita Brookner: Art and Life, which sets the novelist's life beside her art and looks at the efforts to restore her reputation. Only the title reached me, but given how much you enjoy the conversation between painting and fiction, it seems worth a look. In the same spirit, The Paris Review has an essay on Kazuo Ishiguro, called The Butler as Metaphor, about how he inhabits his characters. The excerpt is brief, but it speaks to narrators and the craft of character. And the Southeast Review has a piece on Arundhati Roy's Mother Mary Comes to Me, her memoir of her mother. Again, the text is thin, but the title promises something personal and lyrical, and a formidable mother.

For fiction that teaches history, Literary Hub talks to Mary Beth Keane about Whale Harbor, her fifth novel. It follows the Irish diaspora from County Cork to Galveston in the nineteenth century, and draws on her own family lineage. And if you fancy something for the commute, Backlisted has rerun its 2020 Hallowe'en episode on Beowulf. It's a long, lively conversation comparing the translations by Seamus Heaney, Tolkien, Michael Morpurgo and Maria Dahvana Headley, and how the poem's language has been carried across the centuries.

Now to the galleries. The Guardian reports that a retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham has opened at Tate St Ives, with her large painting Glacier, Blue Cave at its centre. She was long sidelined in the story of St Ives art, and the piece follows her inspirations: glaciers, Vietnam, and her own divorce. Meanwhile, Hyperallergic looks at the major survey of Ana Mendieta at Tate Modern. Her work centres on the earth, the female body, and a practice entirely her own. Two good reasons to think about a trip to Britain.

Next, a little corner for your terminale and the BFI. Hamlet is on the twenty twenty-seven programme, and this morning offers two ways in through adaptation. London Theatre interviews the co-director Steven Hoggett about Hamlet Hail to the Thief, a stage production fusing Shakespeare's play with the music of Radiohead. And Newstrack English has an analysis of Vishal Bhardwaj's film Haider, which reimagines Hamlet in Kashmir. Set side by side, they might make a lively question for a class: what survives when a story changes its music, or its landscape?

From adaptation to documentary. IMDb talks to Matsubayashi Yoju, director of Okinawa Saudade, who spent ten years tracing the island roots of Brazilian dancers. Dance, migration and personal history in one film, which sounds very much your sort of thing. And on ARTE, there is a documentary on the Justice for Magdalenes campaign, which has pressed for the rights of women held in Irish mother-and-baby homes and laundries between nineteen twenty-two and nineteen ninety-six. It is a hard watch, but well documented, and it sits close to novels like Philomena.

Closer to home, two free exhibitions are worth pencilling in. At Allevard, until the third of January, there is Électrique, on the Forges d'Allevard and the rise of hydroelectric white coal, la houille blanche, in the Isère. It is industrial history told through material and place, right on your valley's doorstep. And in Grenoble, until the twenty-fifth of April next year, De tous bois looks at the Hache cabinetmakers and contemporary design, pairing fine woodworking with new creative work. A lovely idea for a weekend, perhaps with a stop at a market on the way.

Now some good news. In New South Wales, after more than a decade of campaigning and three state elections, the Great Koala National Park has been created, the state's second-largest national park. The Optimist Daily explains how carbon credits helped make it possible, which makes it a rather concrete conservation win. And from the same source, a piece of pure wonder: astronomers have identified what is described as the first green star, with the article linking it to the chemistry left behind by a dead planet. A striking image to carry into the evening sky.

And finally, a word for your collection. The Local France offers cauchemardesque, meaning nightmarish, for anyone wanting to add a little theatrical drama to their complaints. Perhaps it suits a Tuesday, or a particularly stubborn pile of marking, though I hope neither is quite that bad.

That's all for this morning, Yamuna. I hope your day has the pleasures of a good first chapter.
